C004.subject: Spiking neural network (SNN) chips
C004.predicate: will achieve at least a 10x energy efficiency improvement over von Neumann architectures within 10 years, but only when inference is performed on event-based sensor data (e.g., DVS cameras) rather than on frame-based video or static datasets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Spiking neural network (SNN) chips von Neumann architectures]

[PATH:empirical] Benchmarking of current-generation SNN chips (e.g., Intel Loihi 2, SynSense Speck) on event-based vision tasks (e.g., DVS gesture recognition, N-Caltech101) against equivalent von Neumann accelerators (e.g., Jetson Orin, Edge TPU) measuring energy per inference and FPS/Watt. — Direct empirical comparison under identical task conditions will quantify whether SNN chips already approach a 10x advantage on event data, and whether the gap is widening over time, providing a concrete test of the hypothesis's core claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical scaling analysis of energy consumption in SNN vs. ANN inference as a function of input sparsity and temporal event density, using models such as the synaptic energy model from Lemaire et al. (2022) or the 'energy-per-synaptic-event' framework. — A rigorous analytical model can predict the maximum possible energy efficiency gain for event-based data versus dense frame-based data, identifying the fundamental limits and whether a 10x improvement is physically plausible within the given timeline.

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review of published power/performance numbers for neuromorphic chips on event-based datasets from 2018–2023, including trends from NeuroBench, IEEE TNNLS surveys, and industry whitepapers. — Aggregating historical data will reveal the trajectory of energy efficiency improvements in SNN hardware, allowing extrapolation to 2033 and assessment of whether the 10x goal is consistent with observed progress rates.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative benchmarking studies of state-of-the-art von Neumann accelerators (e.g., NVIDIA GPU with sparsity and mixed-precision) versus neuromorphic SNN chips (e.g., Intel Loihi 2, IBM TrueNorth) on standard energy-efficiency metrics (e.g., TOPS/W) for representative workloads (e.g., image classification, speech recognition) by 2030-2035. — Direct empirical comparison under consistent conditions would provide quantitative evidence on whether von Neumann architectures can match or exceed SNN energy efficiency, addressing the core claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical projections and architectural simulations of von Neumann efficiency gains from emerging technologies (e.g., near-memory computing, analog in-memory processing, advanced CMOS scaling) versus SNN theoretical limits using analytical models of energy per operation (e.g., based on synaptic vs. von Neumann data movement costs). — Theoretical modeling can reveal fundamental physical and architectural constraints, helping to assess whether von Neumann improvements can plausibly rival SNN efficiencies in the given timeframe.

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review of published energy-efficiency trends for von Neumann processors (e.g., from ISSCC, ISCA, HPCA) and SNN chips (e.g., from NeurIPS, Frontiers in Neuroscience) over the past decade, with extrapolation to 2035. — A comprehensive review of historical and projected efficiency trajectories can identify whether current von Neumann improvements are accelerating, stagnating, or falling short relative to SNN progress, providing context for the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental benchmarking of neuromorphic chips (e.g., Intel Loihi 2, IBM TrueNorth) against equivalent von Neumann processors on standard AI workloads (e.g., spiking neural network inference) with energy-per-inference and FLOPS/watt metrics, published in peer-reviewed venues like IEEE TNNLS or Nature. — Direct measurement of energy efficiency in current neuromorphic systems provides a baseline; if improvements are less than 10x now, projecting 15-year gains requires extrapolation from real hardware data.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of scaling laws for neuromorphic architectures, focusing on the relationship between neuron/synapse density, spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), and energy per spike, compared to CMOS scaling projections for von Neumann systems (e.g., ITRS roadmap). — A formal model can bound the achievable energy efficiency gain given fundamental physical limits (e.g., synaptic energy dissipation, interconnect overhead) and identify whether 10x is plausible without revolutionary device breakthroughs.

[PATH:literature] Literature survey on demonstrated energy efficiency of neuromorphic systems in specialized domains (e.g., sensory processing, robotics) versus general-purpose tasks, including review papers from the IEEE Proceedings or Frontiers in Neuroscience. — Existing evidence may show that neuromorphic gains are largely domain-specific (e.g., event-driven sensors) and not generalizable; this would refute the hypothesis's scope of 'general-purpose' systems achieving 10x improvement.
